title: Parse layer — 3 parser sources, 2 value universes
summary: This layer turns a message body cell into an `mch::Value` that a build program can read as `CAPTURE.body.field`. It is a name -> function-pointer registry fed by three independent sources: 7 hand-written parsers, 22 compiled from `mch-msgs.schema`, and 3 that come out of the Tolk ABI toolchain. The first two sources are pytoniq-parity: they reproduce, deliberately and bug-for-bug, what the Python reference parsers in `indexer/events/blocks/messages/` do — including skipping the leading 32 opcode bits WITHOUT checking them. The third source is tolk-faithful: the generated `from_slice` CHECKS the opcode prefix and models addresses the way `@ton/core` does. Those two conventions are incompatible in observable ways (a missing address is `null` in one and a present-but-empty `Account` in the other), and nothing in the type system keeps them apart — the discipline that does is the op-guard rule at the end of this page. The layer's whole correctness bar is an A/B twin gate: the same corpus through C++ and through the Python engine must produce byte-identical parse dumps.

sections.heading: The registry: three sources, one map, fail-closed
sections.prose:
`MsgParse.h` is short but it is the contract for the entire layer — read its header comment before any code. The registry itself is a lazily-built `std::map<std::string, MsgParserFn>` where `MsgParserFn` is a plain function pointer (`td::Result<Value>(*)(const td::Ref<vm::Cell>&)`), not a `std::function`. That choice is load-bearing later: it is what lets an ABI parser register as an ordinary row with no closure state and no init API.

Three sources merge in a fixed order. Collisions are possible in principle (all three name-spaces are flat), so they are detected once at build time and refused twice: at startup by `validate_registries()`, and at every lookup by `parse_message_body`.

annotations.text: This is the actual specification of the layer, not a courtesy comment. "no opcode validation: the first 32 bits are skipped unchecked" is what makes the pytoniq universe lenient: a body carrying the wrong opcode does not fail, it produces a plausible object built from the wrong bits. Safety comes entirely from the matcher having already checked `op` upstream, in the matcher runtime.

`addr_none` becomes a NULL Value — not an empty address. On this path there is no representation for "present but empty"; a spec that wants to detect addr_none tests for null. Remember this line; the ABI path does the opposite.

"conditionally-present keys" is a real part of the shape: the Python twin sets some attributes only on some code paths, `vars(obj)` is what gets compared, so C++ must omit the key rather than emit a null. The jetton `sum_type` excerpt below is the live case.

The one exception, and the rule it forces. Because ABI parsers validate the prefix and their Python twins do not, an unguarded ABI-path `parse` gives a C++ error and a Python garbage object on the same body — the two sides diverge and the A/B gate fails. Hence: every ABI-path parse capture MUST sit behind an `op` guard.

Seven survivors. Everything else that used to live here was moved to the schema; each of these stayed for a specific irregularity, listed in `mch-msgs.schema`'s NOT GENERATED block. Note `parse_never`: a registered parser that ALWAYS errors, because Python's `JettonBurnNotification` has no `__init__(Slice)` and parity means the parse must always fail.

Meyer's static: the merged registry is built once on first use and is const forever after. No init call to forget, and no static-init-order hazard between the three source accessors — each is itself a function-local static, forced into existence by being called here.

One enumeration of the sources, shared by the merge and the duplicate scan. If the two had their own lists they could drift, and a collision could be silently merged away while the scan reported nothing.
`emplace` (not `insert_or_assign`) is what makes it first-source-wins, and it is silent about it. That silence is precisely why `dups` is computed on the same pass rather than trusted not to happen.

excerpts.title: Duplicate detection and the advisory check

annotations.text: Two sets, not one: `seen` finds a repeat, `dup_set` makes sure a name triple-registered reports once. Output order is first-encounter order, so the startup error message is stable across runs.

Advisory, and deliberately so. The Meyer's-static map cannot itself surface an error, and the engine's no-abort rule forbids dying inside it — so detection lives here while enforcement lives in `parse_message_body` and in `main()`. Nothing on the hot lookup path calls this.

Fail-closed on ambiguity: an ambiguous name errors even though `built.map` does contain an entry for it. The merge resolved the collision by first-wins so the map stays well-formed, but dispatch refuses to act on that arbitrary resolution.
The whole soft-parse contract in one comment: a malformed body must reduce to an ordinary parse failure so the caller can try the next alternative. That is only safe if the catch list is narrow.

And it is narrow on purpose — VM errors plus `std::exception` (what a hand-written tail legitimately throws: out_of_range, logic_error). `bad_alloc` and unknown host faults are NOT caught; they escape to the trace-level handler so an infrastructure failure never masquerades as "this message just isn't that type". This list is also why `AbiBridge` had to stop using `append_cellslice` — see the ABI section.
Placed before mode dispatch on purpose, so the early-returning dump and self-test modes are covered too — the check is worthless if only the production path runs it.

A duplicate key stops the process instead of letting lookups dispatch to whichever source happened to be enumerated first. Since prod is clean today, this branch is dead in practice; its value is that adding a colliding name is a hard startup failure rather than a silent behaviour change.

sections.heading: Universe 1 — pytoniq parity (PSlice and the hand parsers)
sections.prose:
`parse/PSlice.{h,cpp}` is the leaf layer everything in sources 1 and 2 is built from: address, coins, snake-bytes, to-cell. It is not a thin wrapper over `vm::CellSlice` — it exists because pytoniq's `Slice` has behaviours a `CellSlice` does not, and the twin gate compares rendered output, so those behaviours have to be reproduced rather than corrected.

The rest of `PSlice.cpp` beyond the excerpt below is the same kind of work: `load_snake_bytes` (byte-aligned, at most one ref per link), `pslice_to_cell`, and a byte-level reimplementation of Python's `bytes.decode("utf-8", errors="backslashreplace")` used for TON-transfer comments. Read those directly if you touch comments; they are mechanical once the principle is clear.

annotations.text: The reason a bare `vm::CellSlice` is not enough: pytoniq tracks the ref list separately from the bit cursor, and `copy()` does not preserve ref consumption. So `refs` + `off` are carried alongside `cs` and the two cursors are allowed to disagree — reproducing that disagreement is the point.

`to_cell()` means "remaining bits + refs from `off`", i.e. the pytoniq view of what is left, not a copy of the original cell. This is what a `forward_payload` Bytes value is serialized from, so getting `off` wrong changes a payload's root hash.

excerpts.title: load_address_py — where the universe is defined

annotations.text: `addr_none` -> null Value. One line, and it is the fork in the road for the whole layer: on this path "no address" and "absent field" are the same value, and a spec cannot tell them apart.

A zero-length external address is an error only because pytoniq's `ba2int('')` raises. Parity means importing the upstream quirk, not fixing it — a "fix" here shows up as an A/B diff, not as a bug fix.

Why the hand-rolled 32-bit chunk loop instead of `fetch_int256(len,false)`: for lengths 257..511 that returns an invalid-but-non-null RefInt256 that renders as NaN, diverging from Python's exact bigint. The result is the string `extern:<len>:<decimal>` — an ordinary Str, so a spec comparing it against an address field gets a plain mismatch rather than a type error.

`addr_var` errors because pytoniq raises on it. Just past this excerpt, anycast is consumed but never APPLIED — the address prefix is left un-rewritten, unlike `convert::to_raw_address`, so anycast addresses render differently here than elsewhere in the indexer.

One bit decides whether `forward_payload` is a ref or the remainder of this same slice. Both branches end up as a `PSlice`, and the difference between them is entirely in what ref list that PSlice carries.

The single strangest parity quirk in the layer. Python's `Slice.copy()` resets ref consumption, so the INLINE branch sees ALL body refs from index 0 — including the `custom_payload` ref already consumed a few lines above. Reproduced by handing over `ctx.all_refs` with `off = 0` rather than the live cursor. Use the live cursor and the payload cell you serialize has the wrong refs, hence a different root hash.
Fewer than 32 bits left: `sum_type` becomes "Unknown" and `payload_sum_type` is never set. Which keys EXIST is part of the compared shape, so an unconditional null here would be a diff.
Python `hex()` formatting: lowercase, no zero padding, so `0x25938561` but also `0x0`. The rendering itself is data that gets compared — `%08x` would be a diff.
A failed snake read downgrades `sum_type` to "Unknown" instead of failing the parse, because the enclosing Python `try` swallows it. Failure handling is per-branch, not uniform.

The trap this function exists for: on the stonfi-swap SUCCESS path Python never assigns `sum_type`, but on the failure sub-branch it does. `has_sum_type` is a flag that exists purely to reproduce that asymmetry — there is no cleaner formulation that stays byte-identical.

sections.heading: Universe 1, continued — the schema-generated middle source
sections.prose:
Most registered parsers are not written by hand. `mch-msgs.schema` is a small declarative file compiled by `indexer/events/mch/msgs_gen.py` into a committed C++ TU, `MsgParsersGenerated.cpp`. Two constraints make this safe rather than clever: the generator may only emit calls to leaf helpers that already existed and were already A/B-proven, and regeneration must be byte-stable (a pytest re-runs the generator and diffs the committed file).

The generated code lives in the SAME universe as the hand parsers — same leaves, same unchecked opcode skip. The schema is a compression of hand parsers, not a new semantics.

annotations.text: "ALWAYS skipped unchecked" and "never compared" — the opcode in a schema line is documentation plus test-vector filler. Contrast the ABI path, where the prefix IS the parse. Two of the three sources treat the opcode as something someone else already checked.

The rule that keeps the generator honest: every leaf maps 1:1 onto a helper that already existed. New protocols get new compositions, never new parse semantics — which is why the generator could not silently introduce a divergence from the Python twins.
`addr_py`'s three possible outputs on one line: Account, Null, or an `extern:..` Str. Any spec field fed by an address has to tolerate all three.

`fwd_cell_bits` vs `fwd_cell_refs`: identical TL-B shape, different rule for "is there a payload in the remainder" — JettonNotify looks at leftover BITS, PTonTransfer at leftover REFS. The two hand predecessors genuinely differed, so the schema kept both leaves instead of unifying them and breaking one twin.

The skip is re-stated per message and nothing compares against 0x178d4519 — the opcode appears only in the comment. Underflow on the skip is still a parse failure, so a too-short body fails, a wrong-opcode body does not.

The shape of every generated parser: one braced block per field, explicit error-on-underflow, `emplace_back` into a flat Fields vector. Field ORDER is observable (rendered objects are compared), so the generator emits in schema order and the schema order is kept aligned with the Python `__init__` order.
Second source, 22 rows, emitted in schema order. Determinism is a gate, not a nicety: `tests/mch/test_msgs_gen.py` re-runs the generator into a temp file and byte-diffs it against this committed one.

These strings are what a spec writes after `parse X as ...`. They are the PYTHON class names, so renaming a message class on the Python side breaks the twin pairing, not just a C++ build — the registry key is the contract between the two engines.

sections.heading: Universe 2 — the ABI bridge (entry to the tolk world)
sections.prose:
The third source comes from a completely different toolchain: a `.tolk` declaration is compiled to `dedust_v2.abi.json`, which `ton-abi-gen` turns into C++ structs with `from_slice` / `store` / `to_abi_value`. Those structs know nothing about mch — the dependency runs mch -> ton-abi only, permanently.

`AbiBridge` is the whole seam: a function template that adapts `T::from_slice` to a `MsgParserFn`, plus a total `AbiValue -> mch::Value` adapter. Both halves are worth reading closely, because this is where the second value universe gets its shape.

annotations.text: Stated outright: this adapter is NOT pytoniq. Both universes produce the same C++ `Value` type, so the compiler will never object to mixing them — the only thing keeping them apart is the op-guard discipline in the next section.

The trampoline, and why there is no registration API: `&abi_parse_body<T>` is a free function-template instantiation, so its address has EXACTLY `MsgParserFn`'s type. No `std::function`, no closure state, no init step — the type parameter carries the dispatch.

Exotic (pruned/library) cells are rejected here rather than deeper: `load_cell_slice_special` reports specialness, and an exotic body must become a clean Error result. The no-abort rule applies inside parsers as much as anywhere else.

Two calls, and the first is the entire divergence from the other two sources: `from_slice` checks its own prefix. Then `to_abi_value()` flattens the struct into the ABI's own dynamic value, and only then does mch see anything.

`load_and_check_prefix` reads PREFIX_LEN bits and compares them to PREFIX, erroring on mismatch. A wrong-opcode body is a parse ERROR here, exactly where the pytoniq path would have cheerfully returned an object built from the wrong bits.

Straight-line, one field per line, each wrapped by `TRY_RESULT_PREFIX_ASSIGN` so a failure carries `Struct.field:` in the message. Errors name the failing field for free — worth knowing when reading engine logs.
`uint2` is loaded through `load_uint64` with width 2: the generator picks a leaf per C++ storage type and passes the bit width as data, rather than emitting a distinct helper per width.

excerpts.title: adapt_address — the clearest proof the universes differ

annotations.text: Std addresses converge: uppercase raw `wc:HEX`, the same canonical string `load_address_py` builds via `hex_upper`. So an ordinary address compares equal ACROSS universes — which is exactly what makes the other two cases easy to miss.
Here is the split. `addr_none` is a present-but-empty Account, NOT a null Value as on the pytoniq path. A spec that null-tests an ABI-parsed address field is asking a question that can never be true.

External addresses become `Obj{bits, value}` versus pytoniq's `"extern:<len>:<dec>"` string. Same TL-B input, two renderings that will never compare equal — the concrete reason a capture parsed one way cannot be fed to logic written for the other.

`"$"` is emitted FIRST, then declared fields in decl order. Order matters because rendered objects are compared against the Python twin, and the leading `$` gives a consumer a uniform discriminant to switch on.

Only value-carrying union variants reach this branch; struct-labelled variants are Struct-kind and already carry their own `$`. So a union is either `{$, value}` or just the inner struct — two shapes, one discriminant key.

The `v.inner ? ... : null` guard is what makes the adapter TOTAL: no `AbiValue` can drive it into an error or UB. That matters because a throw or error escaping here would be indistinguishable from a parse miss — the adapter is required to be the boring half of the bridge. Same reason `cell_from_slice` (top of the file) uses `append_cellslice_bool`: the throwing overload raises `vm::CellWriteError`, which is neither a `vm::VmError` nor a `std::exception`, so `parse_message_body`'s catch list would NOT have caught it.

BARE decl names, not `<contract>::<decl>` — because the `.mch` grammar's `parse CAP as Name` reads a single IDENT. The price is that every ABI shares one flat key namespace with the other two sources; `validate_registries()` is the backstop, and a real cross-ABI clash is the trigger to revisit this.
Three rows today, all DeDust CPMM V2. Adding an ABI-path protocol is: a line here, plus a Python twin class registered under the same bare name — nothing else in the registry machinery changes.

sections.heading: Why the universes never mix: the op-guard rule
sections.prose:
Both universes hand back an `mch::Value`, and the engine has no way to tell which one produced it. The rule that keeps them from colliding is enforced socially, in spec review: an ABI-path `parse` capture must be bound to a capture that is already `op`-guarded.

The reason is asymmetric failure. The C++ ABI parser CHECKS the prefix and errors on a mismatch; the Python twin skips 32 bits unchecked like everything else in the Python engine. On a body with the right opcode both sides agree. On any other body, C++ produces a parse failure (a Null body, silently) and Python produces a garbage object — and the A/B gate diverges, usually somewhere far away from the parse.

annotations.text: Every capture that gets ABI-parsed below is bound here by an `op` guard first. That ordering is not stylistic: matching runs before building, so by the time `parse claim as ClaimRewardMessage` executes, the body is already known to carry 0x909fdb65 and both engines are guaranteed to agree.

`as ClaimRewardMessage` is resolved by bare name against the registry — C++ finds the ABI bridge row, Python finds a twin class in `Registries.message_types`. The name is the only thing tying the two implementations together.

A parse kept deliberately even though none of its fields are read: it exercises the third parser on both sides so the twin gate covers it. Worth knowing when you wonder why an apparently unused statement is there.

excerpts.title: The Python twin — tolk-faithful, by hand

annotations.text: The asymmetry in one line: the twin skips the opcode unchecked (the pytoniq convention the rest of the Python engine follows) where the C++ side checks the prefix. Same body, different failure mode — this is why the op guard is mandatory rather than advisory.

camelCase attribute names matching the ABI field names, not the TL-B snake_case in the comment above. The twin is deliberately tolk-faithful rather than pytoniq-faithful, because it has to match what the ADAPTER emits.

`AccountId(...)` wrapping matters: `load_address()` returning None yields `AccountId(None)`, which renders as addr_none — matching `Value::make_account_none()` from the adapter. A bare `None` here would be the pytoniq convention and would diff.

The same recipe on the five-field message: `load_coins()` gives a plain int (mirroring the adapter's Int, not an Amount), and every address is wrapped. Names and their ORDER are pinned in an `ABI_FIELDS` table further down this file and checked against the committed `.abi.json` by a pytest — otherwise a rename or reorder on either side would break the twin silently.

sections.heading: How a spec's parse statement actually resolves
sections.prose:
The registry has one real consumer: the build runtime's `parse` statement ([[build-programs]]). Its behaviour explains why a mis-wired ABI parse is quiet rather than loud — a failed parse and a not-this-type parse are the same outcome by design.

There is also a preflight: `BuildDriver` scans every matcher's referenced message types against the registry and build-skips matchers whose types are missing, printing a warning listing them. So a spec referencing a type nobody registered degrades to "this matcher never builds", visible in the skip reasons rather than as a crash ([[ir-artifact]], [[gates]]).

excerpts.title: soft_parse — first alternative that succeeds wins

annotations.text: An unregistered type name is a FAULT (it rejects the whole match), while a failing parser is merely a miss. The distinction is intentional: a typo'd type name is a broken spec, a body that isn't that type is normal traffic.
A missing or undecodable body does not abort the loop — it behaves like Python's `get_body()` raising inside each alternative's own `try`, so alternatives are still consumed in order.

All alternatives failing leaves the body Null, and downstream `.body.field` accesses null-propagate. This is exactly why an unguarded ABI parse is silent on the C++ side: the prefix-check error is indistinguishable from "not this type", and the divergence only surfaces later as a diff against Python.

edges.why: a matcher's parse statements become ref_msgtypes in the IR artifact; those names are resolved against this registry at load time
the op guard that makes an ABI-path parse safe is evaluated here, before any body is parsed
rt_parse / soft_parse is the registry's only production consumer; it defines the parse-failure-equals-null-body contract
the body cell handed to a parser is the base64 message content decoded by the loader — a missing content row is a parse-alternative failure, not an error
the --parse-dump A/B twin gate and the --abi-bridge-test self-test are what hold the parity claims on this page

the schema compiler. Straightforward recursive-descent parse into dataclasses plus string emission; the interesting decisions all live in the schema's own header comment. Only read it if you are adding a LEAF type (~470 LOC)
